claims.title: JWT Signature Verification Disabled

claims.title: JWT Token Accepted Without Cryptographic Verification

` without escaping. The 'note' variable is directly interpolated into HTML. customerName() and footer() correctly use escapeHtml(), but invoiceNote() does not.

claims.title: Medium: Redirect-Based SSRF Bypass
claims.impact: Hostname allowlist bypass: even with fetchAsset() ALLOWED whitelist, an attacker controlling a whitelisted server (e.g., assets.example.com) can redirect to internal URLs, bypassing the allowlist check that happens before the redirect.
claims.evidence: Line 6 in fetchLogo() uses { redirect: 'follow' }, which allows HTTP redirects. The hostname check on line 13 in fetchAsset() occurs BEFORE the fetch and redirect. A URL pointing to 'assets.example.com' that redirects to 'localhost:6379' would pass the whitelist but fetch internal services.

claims.title: JWT Token Verification Bypassed via jwt.decode()
claims.impact: An attacker can forge JWT tokens and impersonate any user, including those with elevated privileges. The jwt.decode() function decodes without signature verification.
claims.evidence: Line 4: 'const claims = jwt.decode(bearer);' does not pass a secret parameter. Line 10 has the same issue. The function should use jwt.verify(token, secret) instead.

claims.title: SQL Injection via ORDER BY Parameter
claims.impact: The 'order' query parameter is directly interpolated into the SQL query without parameterization or validation. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL code by crafting a malicious 'order' parameter, allowing data exfiltration, modification, or deletion from the database.
claims.evidence: Line 16: const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${order}`, ...). The 'order' variable comes from req.query.order with only a default fallback. Contrast with /payments endpoint (line 23) which uses an explicit whitelist SORTABLE[req.query.sort].

claims.title: Missing Authorization Check in GET /invoices/:id Endpoint
claims.impact: An attacker can retrieve invoices belonging to any user by simply changing the invoice ID in the URL. There is no verification that the requesting user is the owner of the invoice. Combined with the JWT forgery vulnerability (F-002), this allows complete unauthorized access to all invoice data in the system. This is a critical data exposure vulnerability.
claims.evidence: Lines 7-10: router.get('/invoices/:id', async (req, res) => { const invoice = await db.query('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]); res.json(invoice); }). The query only checks invoice ID, with no owner_id filter. Compare with the /receipts/:id endpoint (lines 13-19) which correctly includes: WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2 with [req.params.id, req.user.id]. An attacker can request GET /invoices/1, GET /invoices/2, etc., and retrieve all invoices regardless of ownership.

claims.title: JWT Verification Bypass - Unverified Token Decoding
claims.impact: Complete authentication bypass. Attacker can forge JWT tokens with arbitrary claims (user ID, admin role, tenant ID) without any signature verification. Enables unauthorized access to all protected endpoints, privilege escalation to admin, cross-tenant data access, and full account takeover. Multiple occurrences on lines 6 and 12.
claims.evidence: Line 6: `const claims = jwt.decode(bearer);` uses jwt.decode() which only decodes the payload without signature verification. Line 12 contains identical vulnerable pattern. Should use jwt.verify(bearer, secret) instead. The jsonwebtoken library is available but the wrong function is called. Attacker can create unsigned JWT with any claims.

claims.title: node-fetch Version 2.7.0 May Have Known CVEs
claims.impact: Older versions of node-fetch may contain known security vulnerabilities related to HTTP header injection, DNS rebinding, or request smuggling.
claims.evidence: "node-fetch": "2.7.0" in dependencies. This is an older major version (2.x) of node-fetch. Node.js 18+ has built-in fetch; pinning to 2.x may pull in unpatched vulnerabilities.

claims.title: Missing Authentication Middleware on Protected Routes
claims.impact: Routes that should require authentication (all endpoints in this file) reference req.user but no authentication middleware is applied. If req.user is undefined, authorization checks silently fail and all data may be exposed.
claims.evidence: Lines 7-39: Routes reference req.user.id (lines 16, 24, 32) and req.body without any authentication middleware. The auth.js file defines currentUser() but it is never called or used as middleware. Routes are not protected with a middleware chain like app.use(authenticate).

claims.title: Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA/IDOR) on /invoices/:id endpoint
claims.impact: An attacker can enumerate and read invoices belonging to other users by guessing or iterating invoice IDs. There is no ownership check. The /receipts/:id endpoint (line 13-18) correctly implements this check, but /invoices/:id does not.
claims.evidence: Lines 7-10: router.get('/invoices/:id', async (req, res) => { const invoice = await db.query('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]); res.json(invoice); }); - The query only filters by invoice ID, not by owner. Compare to /receipts/:id (lines 13-18): 'SELECT * FROM receipts WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2' with [req.params.id, req.user.id] - this is the correct pattern.

claims.title: JWT decoded without verification allows authentication bypass
claims.impact: An attacker can assume any user's identity and role, accessing any resource the application exposes.
claims.evidence: Lines 6 and 12 use `jwt.decode(bearer)` without calling `jwt.verify()`. Any attacker can forge a JWT with arbitrary claims (sub, role, tenant) and bypass authentication.

claims.title: SQL Injection in Invoice Query - Unparameterized ORDER BY Clause
claims.impact: Allows arbitrary SQL injection through the order parameter, enabling time-based data exfiltration, table modification/deletion, and potential full database compromise via blind SQL injection techniques
claims.evidence: The GET /invoices endpoint constructs SQL with direct string interpolation: SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${order} where order comes from req.query.order without validation. An attacker can inject SQL after ORDER BY, such as: ?order=created_at;DROP TABLE invoices;-- or use CASE statements for blind injection.

claims.title: Missing Authentication on /branding/preview Endpoint
claims.impact: An unauthenticated attacker can access the /branding/preview endpoint, triggering logo fetches on demand. This can be used to probe internal services or amplify SSRF attacks.
claims.evidence: Line 46: 'router.post(\'/branding/preview\', async (req, res) => { const image = await fetchLogo(req.body.logoUrl);' - no middleware or authentication check is present before this handler. The endpoint accepts any request.

claims.title: JWT tokens decoded without signature verification (token forgery)
claims.impact: An attacker can forge JWT tokens with any claims (including admin roles) without knowing the signing secret, leading to authentication bypass and privilege escalation.
claims.evidence: Line 6 uses jwt.decode(bearer) without calling jwt.verify(). The function does not pass a secret key for verification, allowing any attacker to forge tokens with arbitrary claims.

claims.title: SQL Injection in /invoices Endpoint via order Parameter
claims.impact: An attacker can execute arbitrary SQL queries by manipulating the 'order' query parameter, allowing database exfiltration, modification, or deletion.
claims.evidence: Line 20: 'const order = req.query.order || \'created_at\'; ... ORDER BY ${order}' - the order parameter is directly interpolated into the SQL query without any sanitization or parameterization.

claims.title: SQL Injection via ORDER BY Parameter
claims.impact: Attacker can execute arbitrary SQL commands, leading to data exfiltration, modification, deletion, or database compromise
claims.evidence: GET /invoices endpoint takes req.query.order parameter and directly interpolates it into SQL query: `SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${order}`. The order parameter is never validated. Attacker can inject SQL by calling /invoices?order=created_at;DROP TABLE invoices;--

claims.title: BOLA/IDOR on GET /invoices/:id — no ownership verification
claims.impact: Any authenticated user can retrieve any invoice by guessing or enumerating invoice IDs. Invoices contain sensitive financial data (lines 21, 28 show they are user-scoped in other endpoints). An attacker can read all invoices in the system.
claims.evidence: router.get('/invoices/:id', async (req, res) => { const invoice = await db.query('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]); res.json(invoice); }); — Contrast with lines 14-17 where GET /receipts/:id correctly filters by owner_id: 'SELECT * FROM receipts WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2', [req.params.id, req.user.id]. The /invoices endpoint omits the ownership check.

claims.title: SQL Injection in GET /invoices Endpoint
claims.impact: An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL code through the 'order' query parameter, potentially leading to unauthorized data access, modification, deletion, or database corruption. The attacker can bypass access controls and compromise data integrity.
claims.evidence: Line 24: const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${order}`, [req.user.id]); The 'order' variable is derived from req.query.order without validation and directly interpolated into the SQL query string. Example malicious input: ?order=id;DELETE FROM invoices;--

claims.title: SQL Injection via ORDER BY Column Name
claims.impact: SQL injection via ORDER BY clause. Attacker can inject SQL into the order parameter to exfiltrate data, modify queries, or escalate privileges.
claims.evidence: const order = req.query.order || 'created_at'; ... ORDER BY ${order}. User input from req.query.order is directly interpolated into the SQL query string without parameterization or allowlist validation, unlike /payments which uses a SORTABLE allowlist.

claims.title: SQL injection via unparameterized ORDER BY clause
claims.impact: Attacker can inject arbitrary SQL through the 'order' query parameter, potentially exfiltrating all data from the invoices table, modifying data, or executing database functions. Example: ?order=created_at;DROP TABLE invoices;--
claims.evidence: Line 24: db.query(`SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${order}`, [req.user.id]) concatenates req.query.order directly into the SQL string. Unlike the $1 parameter for owner_id, the ORDER BY clause is not parameterized. The /payments endpoint at line 32 uses a SORTABLE allowlist (correct pattern), but /invoices does not.

claims.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via Redirect in fetchLogo
claims.impact: An attacker-controlled logoUrl can redirect to internal services (localhost, internal IPs) or sensitive endpoints, leading to SSRF attacks
claims.evidence: const response = await fetch(url, { redirect: 'follow' }); - allows the server to follow redirects to any destination including internal services

claims.title: High: Stored XSS via Unescaped invoiceNote Function
claims.impact: Stored XSS: attacker can inject JavaScript into invoice notes. If notes are stored in the database and rendered to other users, the payload executes in their browser context, enabling session hijacking, credential theft, and malware distribution.
claims.evidence:
Line 5 returns `
${note}
` without HTML escaping. The parameter 'note' comes from user input and is directly interpolated. The same file correctly escapes customer names on line 10 using escapeHtml(name), demonstrating the function exists and is available. The inconsistency shows invoiceNote() is missing the critical escaping step.

claims.title: SQL injection via unsanitized ORDER BY parameter
claims.impact: An attacker can execute arbitrary SQL, reading, modifying or deleting data, or executing commands on the database server depending on its configuration.
claims.evidence: Line 24: `const order = req.query.order || 'created_at'; ... ORDER BY ${order}`. The `order` parameter is user-supplied and directly interpolated into the SQL query string. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL, e.g., `?order=created_at; DROP TABLE invoices;--`.

claims.title: SQL Injection via Unsanitized ORDER BY Parameter
claims.impact: An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL expressions into the ORDER BY clause, potentially exfiltrating data, bypassing filters, or causing denial of service.
claims.evidence: const order = req.query.order || 'created_at'; const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${order}`, [req.user.id]); The order variable is interpolated directly into SQL without validation.

claims.title: SQL Injection in /invoices endpoint via ORDER BY clause
claims.impact: An attacker can execute arbitrary SQL queries by manipulating the 'order' query parameter, potentially exfiltrating all invoices from all users, deleting data, or executing commands on the database.
claims.evidence: Line 24: const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${order}`, [req.user.id]); - The 'order' variable from req.query.order is interpolated directly into the SQL string without parameterization. The /payments endpoint (line 32) demonstrates the correct pattern using a SORTABLE allowlist.

claims.title: Weak JWT Parsing Allows Null User Context
claims.impact: When jwt.decode() fails (no Bearer token, invalid format), currentUser() returns { id: undefined, role: undefined }. This falsy user object may bypass authorization checks in downstream code if developers use if(req.user) instead of if(req.user?.id). The /receipts/:id endpoint checks owner_id but /invoices/:id endpoint trusts req.user.id being set.
claims.evidence: const claims = jwt.decode(bearer); return { id: claims && claims.sub, role: claims && claims.role }; at lines 5-6. When bearer token is empty or invalid, claims is null/undefined, resulting in { id: undefined, role: undefined }. This passes falsy checks but may not stop queries if not properly validated.
